1. Outside view. What is the base rate here? What has this series done historically, how much does it move between releases, and what would a naive extrapolation predict?
Historically, the Civiqs daily tracker for the percentage of US registered voters who are "angry" about the way things are going has moved slowly, with a mean week-over-week change of 0.31 points. Over the last ten weeks, the series has fluctuated within a tight 1-point band between 29.2 and 30.2, with an average of 29.67. The most recent reading showed a relatively large 0.7-point jump from 29.2 to 29.9. A naive extrapolation relying purely on the most recent number and historical smoothing would predict a value very close to 29.9, perhaps with a slight reversion toward the 10-week mean of ~29.7.

2. Inside view. What is specific to this release -- events, timing, anything that would move this particular number away from the base rate? Say how much each is worth, in the unit of the series.
Search results show recent news focusing on declining approval ratings for President Donald Trump ahead of the upcoming 2026 midterms. Civiqs polling itself was cited for Trump's approval dropping across several states, alongside a general increase in disapproval. This negative sentiment intuitively maps onto an increase in voters feeling "angry" about the direction of the country, which aligns perfectly with the sharp 0.7 jump observed last week (from 29.2 to 29.9). Given the MRP model's smoothing, such a shift represents genuine signal rather than noise. Consequently, we shouldn't expect a complete reversion to 29.2. It's more likely that the tracker will hold steady around these elevated levels or drift slightly as the negative sentiment solidifies in the rolling average. I will adjust slightly downward by 0.1 to account for standard mean-reversion forces after a large single-week spike.

3. Pre-mortem. Assume your answer turns out badly wrong. Write the most likely reason, then correct for it.
If the forecast is badly wrong, it is likely because the 0.7 jump was either an over-reaction by the model to a temporary news cycle (and thus reverts strongly back to ~29.5) or marks the beginning of a larger structural shift heading into the midterms, pushing the number past 30.2 (its highest recent peak). To correct for this, I should not drag the mean too aggressively back to the mid-29s, but I must maintain a standard deviation wide enough to cover both a complete reversion to 29.5 and a continued surge above 30.0. 

4. Calibrate. Your sd should be wide enough that the true value falls inside one sd about two thirds of the time. Check it against how much this series actually moves between releases.
The mean week-over-week change is 0.31 points. A standard deviation of 0.35 is slightly larger than the mean change, giving a 1-SD confidence interval of [29.45, 30.15] around a mean of 29.8. This captures the possibility of a steady hold, a moderate reversion to the historical average, and a slight continuation of the upward trend, which perfectly fits the historical dynamics of the series.
